cards.explanation: The answer is that Laban takes his relatives and chases Jacob. Laban, Jacob's father-in-law, doesn't wait around. He takes his relatives with him and pursues Jacob (Genesis 31:23). Nobody grabs the whole family for a quick errand, friends, so I think he means business.

The answer is False. There's no loophole. God tells Laban, “Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.” (Genesis 31:24). Good and bad are both covered, friends. Laban walks into that camp with his hands tied, and I think he knows it.

The answer is with joy and singing. Laban says he would have sent Jacob away “…with joy and singing, with tambourines and harps.” (Genesis 31:27). That's quite a send-off for somebody he's chasing across the hills now. Whatever he feels, that's the picture he paints.

The answer is False. Laban says, “I have power to do you great harm…” (Genesis 31:29). Then he adds that the God of Jacob's father spoke to him last night. He has the power and he still doesn't use it.

The answer is gods. Laban asks, “But why have you stolen my gods?” (Genesis 31:30). First he names Jacob's longing for his father's house, then he goes straight for the accusation. Keep your eye on those gods, friends, because they're about to matter a lot.

The answer is that the person will not live. Jacob says it straight: “If you find your gods with anyone here, he shall not live!” (Genesis 31:32). That's a heavy thing to say, and the next line explains why it matters: Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen the idols. He promised that without knowing who had them.

The answer is False. The text tells us, “For Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen the idols.” (Genesis 31:32). Rachel is Jacob's wife and Laban's daughter. So Jacob is speaking boldly with the one fact he's missing.

The answer is nothing. Laban goes through Jacob's tent, Leah's tent and the tents of the two maidservants, and “…he found nothing.” (Genesis 31:33). That's four tents and zero idols, friends. Then he leaves Leah's tent and walks into Rachel's (Genesis 31:33). I think that's where Rachel's heart starts pounding.

The answer is in a saddlebag she's sitting on. Rachel “…put them in the saddlebag of her camel, and was sitting on them.” (Genesis 31:34). Hiding something right under yourself is bold. It's like stashing a cookie in your apron pocket and then standing very still.

The answer is True. The text says, “So Laban searched but could not find the household idols.” (Genesis 31:35). He had already looked all through the tent. After Rachel speaks, he's still empty-handed.

The answer is True. Jacob says, “Put it here before my brothers and yours, that they may judge between the two of us.” (Genesis 31:37). He asks whether Laban found anything of his. He wants both families watching, and I think that's a man who's done being quiet about it.
The answer is ate. Jacob says, “…nor have I eaten the rams of your flock.” (Genesis 31:38). He's saying he looked after the flock instead of helping himself. And that's after twenty years.
The answer is False. Jacob says, “I did not bring you anything torn by wild beasts; I bore the loss myself.” (Genesis 31:39). The loss was his. That's a long way from the boss taking it.

The answer is Laban's two daughters. Jacob says, “…fourteen years for your two daughters…” (Genesis 31:41). Those are Rachel and Leah. Fourteen years is a long stretch of service, friends, and Jacob counts every one of them out loud.

The answer is empty-handed. Jacob says, “If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been with me, surely by now you would have sent me away empty-handed.” (Genesis 31:42). He credits God being with him. His hands are full because of that, not because of Laban.

The answer is that they make a covenant. Laban says, “Come now, let us make a covenant, you and I, and let it serve as a witness between you and me.” (Genesis 31:44). He goes from chasing to making an agreement. I think the dream from the night before is still on his mind.

The answer is mound. Jacob tells his relatives, “Gather some stones.” They “…took stones and made a mound…” (Genesis 31:46). Before that, Jacob had set up one stone as a pillar (Genesis 31:45). And the text says they ate there by the mound. A pile of stones and a meal right beside it, I like it.

The answer is witness. Laban declares, “This mound is a witness between you and me this day.” (Genesis 31:48). A pile of stones can't talk, but it can stay put. That's all a witness like that needs to do.

The answer is True. Laban says, “If you mistreat my daughters or take other wives, although no one is with us, remember that God is a witness between you and me.” (Genesis 31:50). Nobody else may be around, but God is. That's the thing he wants Jacob to remember.
The answer is taking other wives. Laban says, “If you mistreat my daughters or take other wives…” (Genesis 31:50). Those are his two conditions, friends. He ties them both to God being a witness.
The answer is False. It's mutual. Laban says, “…I will not go past this mound to harm you, and you will not go past this mound and pillar to harm me.” (Genesis 31:52). Both men are bound by it.

The answer is that Jacob swears by the Fear of Isaac. The text says, “So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.” (Genesis 31:53). Isaac is Jacob's father. Laban talked about the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, and Jacob answered by swearing by the Fear of his own father.

The answer is False. After they ate, “…they spent the night on the mountain.” (Genesis 31:54). Nobody storms off in the dark. Laban got up “Early the next morning…” and then headed home (Genesis 31:55). Seven days of chasing, one meal, one night's sleep. That's a man who needed his rest, and I respect it.

The answer is True. The text says, “Early the next morning, Laban got up and kissed his grandchildren and daughters and blessed them.” (Genesis 31:55). It's the goodbye he mentioned back in verse 28. He gets it in the end.
